blocks.text: **The task.** Implement a dynamic array from scratch on top of a fixed-size block, supporting `get`, `set`, `push`, `pop` and `insert`, with amortised O(1) append.
Three fields: the storage block, how much of it is used, and how much exists.
Both are direct index operations, guarded so that out-of-range access fails loudly rather than returning `undefined`:
Note both check against `length`, not `capacity`. Slots beyond the length exist physically but hold nothing meaningful.
`resize` copies only `length` elements, not `capacity` — the slack is uninitialised and copying it would be wasted work.

The shrink threshold is a quarter, not a half — the anti-thrashing rule from the previous lesson. And `insert` copies **backwards**, from the end toward the gap; going forwards would overwrite each element before it was moved.

items: **push / pop** — O(1) amortised, O(N) on a resize.
**insert / remove at index** — O(N), because of the shift.

blocks.text: You have now built the thing

This class is, in outline, what `Array` in JavaScript, `list` in Python, `vector` in C++ and `ArrayList` in Java all are. Real implementations add growth tuning, memory reuse and type specialisation — but the structure is exactly this.
Every cost in that table traces back to the first lesson of the course: memory is a contiguous, addressable line, and everything follows from that.
